summary: Explores how Segment Routing over IPv6 Segment Identifiers relate to the IPv6 Addressing Architecture, since SIDs look and often act like IPv6 addresses. It also allocates a dedicated prefix for SRv6 SIDs. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Segment Routing over IPv6 puts its instructions straight into the IPv6 destination address, so ordinary routers in the middle have to forward packets to those addresses even though they are not normal host addresses. This RFC explains why that is acceptable, and reserves a block of address space so that everyone can recognise and filter traffic belonging to Segment Routing.

questions: what is the srv6 sid format loc funct arg
subtitle: A dedicated IPv6 prefix block for SRv6 Segment Identifiers.

tldr.problem: SRv6 Segment Identifiers appear in the IPv6 Destination Address but do not follow the structure the IPv6 addressing architecture defines, which leaves unclear how ordinary routers should treat them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC clarifies that SIDs are routing prefixes used for forwarding rather than interface addresses, and allocates the 5f00::/16 block as a dedicated space where SRv6 SIDs can be recognised and told apart from ordinary IPv6 addresses.
tldr.outcome: Operators can use the allocated block to filter at the edges of their SR domains, which makes it simpler for a domain to fail closed and keeps SRv6 traffic from leaking in or out.

facts.label: Segment list entry size
facts.value: 128 bits, a contiguous array of IPv6 addresses

today: RFC 9602 is an Informational RFC published in October 2024 and has not been obsoleted. It remains the source of the 5f00::/16 allocation recorded in the IANA IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registry, and it asks the SRv6 operational community to write the conventions and guidelines for using that block.

sections.title: Why SIDs Need Their Own Address Space
sections.content:
Segment Routing over IPv6 uses IPv6 as the underlying data plane. In SRv6, the source node starts a packet with a Segment Identifier in the Destination Address of the IPv6 header, and segment endpoint nodes process a local segment present in that Destination Address. SIDs in SRv6 therefore can, and do, appear in the Destination Address of IPv6 datagrams by design. This document explores the characteristics of SRv6 SIDs and focuses on their relationship to the IPv6 Addressing Architecture, and it allocates and makes available a dedicated prefix for SRv6 SIDs.

The allocation has a stated purpose. All of the SRv6-related specifications discussed are intended to apply to a contained SR domain or between collaborating SR domains. Nodes inside or outside those domains that are not SR-aware will not perform any special behaviour for SRv6 SIDs and will treat them solely as IPv6 routing prefixes. As an added factor of security, it is desirable to allocate some address space that explicitly signals that the addresses within that space cannot be expected to comply with the IPv6 addressing architecture. There is precedent for mechanisms that use IPv6 addresses in a manner different from that specified, and such a block is useful in identifying and potentially filtering packets at the edges of the SR domains, which makes it simpler for the domain to fail closed.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers that do not understand Segment Routing still have to forward these packets, because the destination address is the only thing they can look at. Giving Segment Routing its own reserved block of address space means a plain router, or a filter at the edge of a network, can spot such a packet and handle it deliberately rather than by accident.

sections.title: SIDs Are Routing Prefixes, Not Interface Addresses
sections.content:
The SRH Segment List is defined as a contiguous array of 128-bit IPv6 addresses, and each element of the list is a SID. But the elements are not all equal. Some may represent a local interface, described as a forwarding table entry that represents a local interface and is not locally instantiated as an SRv6 SID. It follows that not all the SIDs appearing in the list are SRv6 SIDs as defined by the Segment Routing architecture. The non-SRv6-SID elements are simply IPv6 addresses assigned to local interfaces, and they need to conform to the IPv6 addressing architecture; the discussion applies solely to SRv6 SIDs that are not assigned to local interfaces.

One key question is how these SRv6 SIDs, appearing as IPv6 Destination Addresses, are perceived and treated by transit nodes, that is, nodes not required to be capable of processing a Segment or the Segment Routing Header. The format of an SRv6 SID is composed of three parts, LOC:FUNCT:ARG, where a locator is encoded in the L most significant bits of the SID, followed by F bits of function and A bits of arguments. If L plus F plus A is less than 128, the argument part is followed by enough zero bits to fill the 128-bit SID. Such an SRv6 SID is assigned to a node within a prefix defined as a Locator of length L. When an SRv6 SID occurs in the Destination Address of an IPv6 header, only the longest matching prefix corresponding to the Locator is used by the transit node to forward the packet to the node identified by the Locator.

It is clear that this format is not compliant with the requirements set out in the IPv6 addressing architecture for IPv6 addresses, but it is also clear that SRv6 SIDs are not intended for assignment onto interfaces on end hosts. They look and act like other mechanisms that use IPv6 addresses with different formats, such as the IPv6 addressing of translators and the ORCHIDv2 prefix for overlay routable cryptographic hash identifiers.

Looking at transit nodes, it becomes apparent that these addresses are used purely for forwarding and not for packet delivery to end hosts. The relevant specification is therefore BCP 198, which requires implementations to support the use of variable-length prefixes in forwarding while explicitly decoupling IPv6 routing and forwarding from the IPv6 address and prefix semantics of the IPv6 addressing architecture. BCP 198 does not override the rules of that architecture; it merely limits where their impact is observed. Furthermore, in the SRv6 specifications all SIDs assigned within a given Locator prefix are located inside the node identified by the Locator, so there does not appear to be a conflict with the subnet-router anycast rules, since such addresses are neither required nor useful within a node.
sections.plainLanguage: A SID is not an address of a machine's interface. It is a routing instruction with three parts: which node it points at, what that node should do, and any argument for that action. A router in the middle only cares about the first part and uses it as a prefix to forward on. The IPv6 addressing rules were written for addresses that reach a host, so they do not fit, and the document explains why that is fine.

sections.title: Compressed SIDs
sections.content:
The compressed-SID encoding introduces a way to use a single entry in the Segment List as a container for multiple SIDs. A node taking part in this mechanism uses the argument part of the Destination Address of the IPv6 header to derive a new Destination Address, so the Destination Address field of the packet changes at a segment endpoint in a way similar to how the address changes as the result of processing a segment in the SRH.

The key point is that the Locator Block at the beginning of the address is not modified by the operations needed for supporting compressed SIDs. Since SRv6 SIDs are treated simply as routing prefixes on transit nodes within the SR domain, this does not constitute a modification to the IPv6 data plane on those transit nodes: any changes are restricted to SR-aware nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: Compressed SIDs pack several instructions into one slot in the segment list, using the argument part of the address to work out the next destination. The block at the front of the address, the part that says which node to go to, stays untouched, so ordinary routers in the path see no difference at all.

sections.title: The Allocated Prefix
sections.content:
Further specifications are needed to describe the conventions and guidelines for the use of the newly allocated address block. The SRv6 operational community, which is the first intended user of the block, is requested to come up with such conventions and guidelines in line with their requirements. At the time of writing, global DNS SHOULD NOT reference addresses assigned from this block.

IANA has assigned the address block 5f00::/16 for the purposes described and recorded it in the IANA IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registry. The name of the allocation is Segment Routing (SRv6) SIDs, the RFC is RFC 9602, and the allocation date is April 2024. The termination date is not applicable. The address block is marked true for source, destination and forwardable, and false for globally reachable and reserved by protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The block is 5f00::/16, reserved in the IANA registry of special-purpose IPv6 addresses and marked as not globally reachable, so it is for use inside networks rather than on the public Internet. The document asks the Segment Routing community to write the operating rules for it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations for the use of Segment Routing, of SRv6 and of SRv6 network programming apply to the use of these addresses. The use of IPv6 tunnelling mechanisms, including SRv6, also brings up the additional concerns described in the security considerations for IP tunnelling. The usage of the prefix allocated by this document improves security by making it simpler to filter traffic at the edge of the SR domains.

In case deployments do not use the allocated prefix, additional care needs to be exercised at network ingress and egress points so that SRv6 packets do not leak out of SR domains and do not accidentally enter SR-unaware domains. Similarly, the SR domain needs to be configured to filter out packets entering it that use the selected prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: Reserving the block is itself a security measure: an edge filter can recognise a Segment Routing packet and drop it if the traffic is not supposed to be there. Without the block, operators have to spot such packets by other means, and packets can leak out of a Segment Routing domain into a network that does not understand them.
